items.title: I Made Invisible Grid Paper… and It Actually Works
items.description: I wanted a portable way to sketch projects on regular paper while still having a grid available when I needed it. The solution turned out to be surprisingly simple: a battery-powered light pad combined with a transparent grid sheet. Put the grid under your paper, turn on the light, and you have instant grid paper. Turn the light off and you're back to a clean drawing with no printed grid lines. In this video I test the setup by sketching one of my recent concrete projects, try drawing with it in a dark room, and talk about a few things I like—and a couple things I would change. The funny part is that the inexpensive transparent grid may actually be my favorite part of the whole setup. Could you use this for woodworking plans, electronics layouts, 3D printing, templates, tracing, or something completely different? Let me know what you would use it for. items.title: I Turned a $1 Thrift Store Ice Tray Into a Concrete Factory
items.description: Yesterday I found a silicone ice cube tray at a thrift store for just $1, so naturally I decided to see if I could turn it into a tiny concrete manufacturing system. In this build I use 3D printing to design a custom insert, create a negative mold, cast that part in two-part silicone, and then use the finished silicone tooling to make repeatable concrete castings. The finished product is, of course, a completely innocent concrete fountain pen holder. Definitely a pen holder. But the bigger experiment is whether 3D printing can be used for more than making finished parts. By using a printer to create masters, molds, jigs, and tooling, one printed design could potentially produce dozens or hundreds of cast products. Can cheap thrift-store finds, 3D printing, silicone, and concrete become a realistic form of small-scale home manufacturing? That’s something I plan to test a lot more. If you enjoy 3D printing, electronics, unusual tools, thrift-store finds, experiments, and DIY builds, consider subscribing to Sawdust & Circuits.

items.title: I Tested the Weird Frequencies You Told Me To Try
items.description: You suggested the frequencies… so today I’m testing them. From 6 Hz and the famous 7.8 Hz Schumann resonance all the way up to 21,000 Hz, we're running through some of the strangest frequency suggestions from the comments. Some are associated online with relaxation, pain relief, tinnitus, the so-called “God frequency,” healing frequencies… and apparently even growing teeth. Yeah. We’re testing that one too. I originally planned to make this a visual experiment using sand, vibration tables, a bass shaker and a 10-inch subwoofer. Unfortunately, the sand had absolutely no interest in cooperating. So we changed plans. In this video we'll test: 6 Hz 7.8 Hz 20 Hz 174 Hz 528 Hz 963 Hz 1,000 Hz 6,111 Hz 21,000 Hz We’ll also talk about what people claim these frequencies do and separate the interesting real science from some of the more questionable internet mythology. Have another strange frequency I should test? Leave the frequency AND what you think it supposedly does in the comments. I may include your suggestion in the next experiment. Thanks for watching Sawdust & Circuits! #Frequency #schumannresonance #soundexperiment #SawdustAndCircuits #scienceexperiment #528Hz #healingfrequencies #audioexperiment

items.title: Novice vs. Work Sharp: Can I Save This Knife?
items.description: Today’s project starts with ruining a perfectly good knife—and then trying to bring it back. In this video, I test the Work Sharp Original Knife & Tool Sharpener, a compact electric belt sharpening system designed for knives, scissors and other edged tools. Instead of judging sharpness by shaving paper or arm hair, I built a 3D-printed cutting fixture and used a Dillon force gauge to measure how much force each blade needed to cut through fishing line. We begin with a utility razor blade as our baseline, test the knife while dull, damage the edge even further and then see whether a complete sharpening novice can restore it with the Work Sharp. The knife begins at approximately 8.8 newtons, improves to 7 newtons after the first sharpening attempt and eventually reaches an impressive 2.2 newtons. Can a tiny belt sander really make a damaged knife sharper than our razor-blade baseline? Let me know what you think of this sharpness-testing method and what material you would use for the next version of the test fixture. Thanks for watching, and I’ll see you next time. **Sawdust & Circuits** #worksharp #knifesharpening #toolreview

items.title: This Phone Mount Has a Refrigerator Built Inside
items.description: Can a tiny refrigerator keep your phone from overheating? In this video, I test a magnetic thermoelectric phone cooler that combines a Peltier module, heatsink, fan, magnetic mount, and—as required by modern technology—RGB lighting. We’ll look at how a Peltier cooler works, watch one through a thermal camera, and compare it with another thermoelectric device: a heat-powered wood-stove fan. Then we’ll attach the cooler to a phone and find out whether it can genuinely reduce temperatures or whether the cold air coming through the car vent is doing most of the work. These coolers may be useful during gaming, wireless charging, GPS navigation, high-resolution video recording, or extremely hot weather—but they also use extra power, create heat on the opposite side, and may introduce condensation under the right conditions. Is this a practical solution for phone overheating or an unnecessarily complicated RGB fan? Let me know what you think in the comments. Thanks for watching, and I’ll see you next time! #phonecooler #PeltierCooler #thermalcamera #SawdustAndCircuits #techreview

items.title: I Tested the “God Frequency” With an Oscilloscope
items.description: Can certain frequencies improve sleep, repair DNA, summon ghosts or even connect you to a higher consciousness? Today on Sawdust & Circuits, I test a Schumann resonance generator using an oscilloscope to see what this strange little wooden box is actually producing. We’ll look at the famous 7.83 Hz Schumann resonance, the 19 Hz “ghost frequency,” 40 Hz brain stimulation, 432 Hz tuning, the 528 Hz “DNA repair” frequency, the 963 Hz “God frequency,” and even the legendary brown note. Some of these frequencies are connected to real science. Others appear to be folklore, spiritual beliefs or very creative marketing. Does the frequency shown on the display match the real output? Does the moving bearing actually react to the selected signal? And is this a useful relaxation device—or just snake oil with a keypad? Watch to the end for the oscilloscope results and my final verdict. What strange frequency should I test next? items.title: I Designed a Bambu AMS Adapter for Small Filament Spools
items.description: Welcome back to **Sawdust and Circuits!** If you've ever tried using small filament spools or sample rolls with the **Bambu Lab AMS**, you've probably run into the same problem—they don't fit like standard spools. Instead of manually respooling every roll, I decided to design my own solution. In this video I design and test a **3D printed small spool adapter** that securely grips smaller filament spools with flexible spring arms, allowing them to feed through the AMS like a standard-sized spool. Along the way I share a bit of my 10-year 3D printing journey—from my first Dremel 3D printer to my current Bambu Lab P1S—and explain why learning CAD has been one of the most valuable skills I've picked up. To test the design, I print a few of my earliest creations using thrift-store filament finds to see if the adapter can reliably handle smaller spools.
